title: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccine recommendations for adults: a review of available global, regional, and country level recommendations

analysis.scope_and_question: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) can cause serious disease in older adults (OAs), particularly those with underlying medical conditions. RSV morbidity, mortality, and health care burden are increasingly evident. We categorized guidance by age, risk factors and comorbidities. We compared differences in indications, age thresholds, and frameworks.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The set cutoff date was November 2025. We examined global implementation of RSV vaccination recommendations by extracting guidelines from national immunization technical advisory groups, ministries of health, global and regional recommendations, and local medical societies.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: It can lead to acute respiratory illness and lower respiratory tract infections in adults ≥60 years and at increased risk groups. Across >24 countries and >50 medical societies, a common recommendation supports RSV vaccination in ≥60 years and immunocompromised individuals. Global guidance converges on prioritizing vaccination for OAs and individuals at high risk of severe disease.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: However, significant heterogeneity exists across countries in age threshold indications and risk-based eligibility, as well as in implementation depending on health system infrastructure and resources.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: This review aims to equip clinicians with practical guidance to support consistent implementation of RSV vaccination recommendations. By synthesizing worldwide RSV vaccination recommendations, this review offers clinicians an accessible guide to support consistent RSV vaccination.

analysis.summary_en: This review examines RSV vaccine recommendations for adults globally, focusing on older adults (OAs) and those at increased risk of severe disease. The analysis highlights that RSV can cause serious illness in adults ≥60 years and those with underlying conditions, leading to acute respiratory illness and lower respiratory tract infections. A common recommendation across >24 countries and >50 medical societies supports vaccination for OAs and immunocompromised individuals. Despite this consensus, significant heterogeneity exists in age thresholds, risk-based eligibility, and implementation, influenced by health system infrastructure and resources. The review aims to provide clinicians with practical guidance to ensure consistent application of RSV vaccination recommendations, offering an accessible synthesis of worldwide guidelines.

title: Enhanced respiratory syncytial virus surveillance of young children admitted to the Sydney Children's Hospitals Network, 2019-2023.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to comprehensively describe the clinical characteristics, management and outcomes of children with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) disease admitted to the Sydney Children's Hospitals Network, determine the full burden of severe disease and identify population-specific risk factors for intensive care unit (ICU) admission.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was a multi-centre, retrospective cohort study conducted over 5 years at two tertiary paediatric hospitals in metropolitan New South Wales, Australia, before implementation of government-funded immunisation programs against RSV in children. Participants included children aged <2 years hospitalised with laboratory-confirmed RSV from 1 January 2019 to 31 December 2023, comprising all ICU admitted and a random sample of non-ICU admitted patients.
analysis.methods: The study involved examining the characteristics and incidence rate of RSV hospitalisations and ICU admissions among children aged <2 years. Factors associated with higher odds of ICU admission were identified using multivariate logistic regression.
analysis.main_results: Over a 5-year period, 4414 children were hospitalised with laboratory-confirmed RSV, of whom 11.3% (499/4414) were admitted to ICU. The median age was younger in the ICU cohort (n = 499) compared with the non-ICU sample (n = 1000; 3.3 vs 7.1 months, P < 0.0001).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as indicating that RSV immunisation programs are expected to substantially reduce the burden of hospitalisation among Australian children in their first year of life. They also noted that children who are Indigenous, were born prematurely or have heart disease are at greatest risk of severe disease and may benefit from extended preventative programs.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the development of targeted preventative programs for high-risk groups, such as Indigenous children, those born prematurely and those with cardiac disease, to reduce the burden of RSV hospitalisations.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was conducted before the implementation of government-funded immunisation programs, which may limit its ability to assess the impact of such programs. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the retrospective design and potential for unmeasured confounding.

analysis.summary_en: This study conducted a multi-centre, retrospective cohort analysis of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) hospitalisations among children under two years of age in Sydney Children's Hospitals Network from 2019 to 2023. It found that 11.3% of RSV hospitalisations required ICU admission, with younger age, prematurity, Indigenous identity, and cardiac disease being significant risk factors. The results suggest that RSV immunisation programs could substantially reduce hospitalisation rates, particularly among high-risk groups. The study's moderate evidence strength is due to its retrospective design and potential for unmeasured confounding, which may limit the generalisability of findings.

title: Human Metapneumovirus in the Post-pandemic Era:: A Multicenter Comparative Study With Respiratory Syncytial Virus in Argentina, 2022–2025

analysis.research_question_and_background: Human metapneumovirus (hMPV) is an important cause of acute lower respiratory infections (ALRI) in children worldwide, and comparative data between hMPV and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in the post-pandemic period remain scarce in Latin America, particularly after the introduction of maternal RSV immunization.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A prospective multicenter surveillance study was conducted in 5 tertiary pediatric hospitals in Argentina between 2022 and 2025, including children hospitalized with reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction-confirmed hMPV or RSV-associated ALRI.
analysis.methods: Epidemiologic characteristics, clinical presentation, respiratory support requirements, outcomes and seasonal patterns were compared, and independent predictors of hMPV versus RSV infection were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression.
analysis.main_results: Among 19,021 ALRI hospitalizations, 661 (3.5%) were hMPV and 2397 (12.6%) were RSV cases. hMPV patients were older (median 10 vs 8 months; P < 0.001), had more comorbidities (59% vs 47%; P < 0.001) and had prior respiratory hospitalizations (42% vs 20%). Fever was more frequent in hMPV (74% vs 65%; P < 0.001), and focal pneumonia predominated over bronchiolitis. RSV required more advanced respiratory support. Mortality was extremely low and comparable. hMPV peaked later than RSV.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study highlights that hMPV demonstrates distinct epidemiologic and clinical characteristics, predominantly affecting older children with respiratory vulnerability.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: In the era of RSV prevention strategies, hMPV may represent an increasingly important contributor to the residual burden of severe pediatric ALRI, highlighting the need for development of preventive interventions.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its observational design and potential confounding factors, but the evidence is strong due to the large sample size and comprehensive analysis.

analysis.summary_en: This study compares human metapneumovirus (hMPV) and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in the post-pandemic era in Argentina. It highlights that hMPV is a significant cause of acute lower respiratory infections (ALRI) in children, with distinct epidemiologic and clinical features compared to RSV. The findings suggest that hMPV predominantly affects older children with respiratory vulnerability and may contribute to the residual burden of severe pediatric ALRI despite low mortality rates. The study's large sample size and comprehensive analysis provide strong evidence, though its observational design introduces potential limitations.

title: Incidence and risk factors of acute respiratory illness associated with influenza, COVID-19, and respiratory syncytial virus within a birth cohort study

analysis.research_question_and_background: Influenza virus, severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) are leading causes of acute respiratory infections (ARIs) in early childhood, yet current understanding is largely reliant on hospital-based surveillance that underestimates the broader community burden.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study analyzed data from 843 participants aged between 0 and 4 years enrolled in the Southern Hemisphere Influenza and Vaccine Effectiveness Research and Surveillance 3 (SHIVERS-III) birth cohort, a longitudinal community-based study in New Zealand, during 2020-2024.
analysis.methods: Nasal swabs were collected from symptomatic participants and tested for viral RNA by RT-PCR. Incidence rates (IRs) and incidence rate ratios (IRRs) were estimated for the surveillance period and adjusted for age, sex, ethnic group, socioeconomic status, and influenza vaccination status.
analysis.main_results: From 2021 to 2024, RSV had the highest incidence rate (63.2/100 person-years [PY]; 95% CI, 56.6-69.8), followed by SARS-CoV-2 (39.3/100 PY; 95% CI, 34.5-44) and influenza (35.7/100 PY; 95% CI, 29-42.3).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Age influenced infection risk: infants <6 months had the lowest incidence of influenza and RSV, potentially reflecting maternally derived immunity and limited exposure. Risk increased after 6 months of age, peaking at age 1 year for RSV and at age 2 years for influenza.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings strengthen the evidence base for age-targeted immunization strategies and improve understanding of early-life respiratory virus epidemiology.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report limitations specific to the study design or analysis methods.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the incidence and risk factors of acute respiratory illness associated with influenza, SARS-CoV-2, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) within a birth cohort of children aged 0-4 years in New Zealand. The research highlights the impact of pandemic-related disruptions on viral circulation and provides insights into age-specific infection risks. RSV was found to have the highest incidence rate during the surveillance period, followed by SARS-CoV-2 and influenza. The study also demonstrates that influenza vaccination reduces the risk of symptomatic influenza. The findings suggest that age plays a significant role in infection risk, with infants under 6 months showing lower rates due to potential maternal immunity. These results contribute to the understanding of early-life respiratory virus epidemiology and support the development of age-targeted immunization strategies. The evidence is based on community-based surveillance and is considered moderate in strength due to the absence of reported limitations.

title: Human metapneumovirus-associated ARI hospitalisation rates in comparison to respiratory syncytial virus and influenza in eastern China, 2020-2024: a time-series analysis.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to estimate the hospitalisation rates of human metapneumovirus (hMPV)-associated acute respiratory infections (ARI) in eastern China and compare them directly with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and influenza during 2020-2024.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A time-series analysis was conducted using a large regional medical database, examining weekly ARI hospitalisations and viral test-positives for hMPV, RSV, and influenza by age group and region in eastern China from 2020 to 2024.
analysis.methods: Negative binomial regression models with natural cubic splines and time-offsets for viral activity were used, excluding patients with COVID-19 and adjusting for the impact of COVID-19 waves.
analysis.main_results: hMPV was associated with 100,792 (5.35%) ARI hospitalisations, RSV with 266,826 (14.17%), and influenza with 409,599 (21.76%). RSV hospitalisations rebounded first in 2021/2022, followed by hMPV in 2022/2023, while influenza hospitalisations increased annually. hMPV- and influenza-associated hospitalisations shifted towards those aged 5-19 years, while RSV-associated hospitalisations shifted towards those aged ≥5 years.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings highlight the distinct age-related patterns of hMPV and RSV hospitalisations, with hMPV showing a higher burden in infants aged 0-5 months and 6-11 months, and RSV and influenza having higher rates in younger age groups.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results provide critical insights for targeted surveillance, diagnosis, and intervention strategies, particularly for infants and young children, to mitigate the burden of hMPV and RSV infections.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study relies on a regional medical database and excludes patients with COVID-19, which may limit generalisability. The evidence is moderate due to the observational nature of the time-series analysis.

analysis.summary_en: This study estimates the hospitalisation rates of human metapneumovirus (hMPV)-associated acute respiratory infections (ARI) in eastern China and compares them with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and influenza during 2020-2024. Using a regional medical database and negative binomial regression models, the analysis excludes patients with COVID-19 and adjusts for its impact. Results show hMPV was associated with 100,792 (5.35%) ARI hospitalisations, RSV with 266,826 (14.17%), and influenza with 409,599 (21.76%). RSV hospitalisations rebounded first in 2021/2022, followed by hMPV in 2022/2023, while influenza hospitalisations increased annually. The findings indicate distinct age-related patterns, with hMPV and influenza affecting older children more, and RSV affecting those aged ≥5 years. The study supports the development of hMPV-specific interventions and highlights the need for targeted public health strategies. However, the reliance on a regional database and exclusion of COVID-19 patients may limit generalisability, resulting in moderate confidence in the evidence.

title: Respiratory Syncytial Virus: reflections on its clinical and economic impact in infant primary care. Authors reply.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to describe the clinical and economic burden of microbiologically confirmed respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections in real-world primary care settings, addressing the need to understand the impact of RSV on healthcare systems and pediatric populations.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A prospective cohort study was conducted in primary care settings, enrolling participants from November 2021 to January 2024. The exposure variable was microbiological confirmation of RSV infection, and the study focused on children under 5 years of age.
analysis.methods: The study involved the collection of clinical and economic data from primary care records, with microbiological confirmation of RSV infection serving as the exposure variable. The enrollment period was chosen to avoid peak periods of SARS-CoV-2 cases, and the analysis included the examination of codetection with SARS-CoV-2.
analysis.main_results: Only 12 samples (2.32%) were positive for SARS-CoV-2, with codetection of RSV/SARS-CoV-2 in 3 (0.76%) cases. The study highlighted the excessive use of bronchodilators in RSV-related cases.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors acknowledge the impact of the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic on RSV epidemiology and note that the study's focus was on describing the burden of RSV rather than assessing prognostic factors. They emphasize the importance of considering the post-pandemic context in their findings.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide insights into the clinical and economic impact of RSV in primary care, which can inform resource allocation and healthcare planning for pediatric respiratory infections.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's design was limited by the lack of uniform documentation of SARS-CoV-2 infection history and the post-pandemic context affecting patient recruitment. The evidence is moderate due to these limitations.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to describe the clinical and economic burden of microbiologically confirmed respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections in primary care settings for children under 5 years. A prospective cohort study was conducted from November 2021 to January 2024, focusing on RSV infection as the exposure variable. The study found that only 12 samples (2.32%) were positive for SARS-CoV-2, with codetection of RSV/SARS-CoV-2 in 3 (0.76%) cases. The authors interpreted these findings as highlighting the excessive use of bronchodilators in RSV-related cases and acknowledged the post-pandemic context affecting the study's design and patient recruitment. The results suggest the need for better resource allocation and healthcare planning for pediatric RSV infections. However, the study's evidence is considered moderate due to limitations in documenting SARS-CoV-2 infection history and the influence of the pandemic on the study's context.

title: Under pressure: lessons learnt from rapid implementation of the respiratory syncytial virus maternal vaccine and infant nirsevimab in Sydney, Australia.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to share lessons from the rapid implementation of RSV prevention products and present data on immunisation uptake for mothers and babies in two maternity hospitals. The research addresses the need for effective strategies to improve RSV vaccine and nirsevimab adoption in clinical settings.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved the rollout of the RSV maternal vaccine and the injectable monoclonal antibody nirsevimab in two maternity hospitals within the Sydney Local Health District. It examined immunisation uptake over a period from February to September 2025.
analysis.methods: Deidentified summary data from electronic medical records were analysed descriptively as counts and proportions. The Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research was used to evaluate the rollout process.
analysis.main_results: RSV vaccination coverage in women giving birth in the two hospitals increased from 4% in the first month of rollout to 70-74% from June to September 2025. The number of live born babies requiring nirsevimab decreased as antenatal coverage improved. Among eligible newborns, 36% of families declined nirsevimab, with reasons for refusal not recorded. Documentation of RSV immunisation status improved during the rollout.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as demonstrating the importance of multidisciplinary engagement and clear messaging in the successful rollout of RSV prevention programs. The study highlights the challenges and strategies for integrating multiple immunisation products into routine clinical practice.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the development of future RSV prevention programs by emphasizing the need for coordinated efforts, clinician education, and systematic safeguards to ensure accurate implementation. They also provide insights into improving immunisation uptake and documentation in maternity settings.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on deidentified summary data and the absence of recorded reasons for nirsevimab refusal. The evidence is moderate, as it reflects real-world implementation challenges but lacks deeper causal analysis or control groups.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the rollout of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) prevention products, including the maternal vaccine and the monoclonal antibody nirsevimab, in two maternity hospitals in Sydney, Australia. It reports that RSV vaccination coverage among mothers improved significantly from 4% in February 2025 to 70-74% by September 2025. The number of infants requiring nirsevimab decreased as maternal coverage increased, while 36% of eligible newborns declined the antibody without recorded reasons. The authors highlight the importance of multidisciplinary collaboration, clinician education, and integrating immunisation into medical workflows for successful program adoption. They note that while the rollout was effective, the study lacks detailed causal analysis and control groups, limiting the strength of the evidence to a moderate level.

title: Bacterial co-infection in patients hospitalized with respiratory syncytial virus and influenza a infection: a retrospective observational cohort study

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to compare the prevalence, microbiological characteristics, and clinical impact of bacterial co-infection in adults hospitalized with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) or influenza A infection.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective observational cohort study was conducted on adults hospitalized with laboratory-confirmed RSV or influenza A infection in Central Denmark between 2015 and 2023.
analysis.methods: Bacterial co-infection was identified using bacterial culturing and urinary antigen testing. Poisson regression was used to estimate risk ratios for bacterial co-infection, and Cox proportional hazards regression was used to evaluate associations between bacterial co-infection and adverse clinical outcomes.
analysis.main_results: Among 4,537 patients, 1,394 had RSV infection and 3,143 had influenza A infection. Among patients undergoing microbiological testing, bacterial co-infection was identified in 187/611 (30.6%) RSV-infected patients and 298/947 (31.5%) influenza A-infected patients (p = 0.72). Among all patients, bacterial co-infection was identified in 187/1,394 (13.4%) RSV infected patients and 298/3,143 (9.5%) influenza A infected patients (p < 0.01). Haemophilus influenzae was the most common pathogen in both groups, followed by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Moraxella catarrhalis and Staphylococcus aureus.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings indicate that bacterial co-infection occurs at similar rates in patients hospitalized with RSV and influenza A infection, and that Haemophilus influenzae is the most frequently isolated bacteria in both groups.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results suggest that empirical antibiotic therapy should consider covering pathogens with beta-lactamase production when bacterial co-infection is suspected in RSV and influenza A infected patients.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and potential for selection bias, but the evidence is strong due to the large sample size and use of statistical methods to evaluate associations.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated bacterial co-infection in adults hospitalized with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) or influenza A infection. It found that bacterial co-infection occurred at similar rates in both viral groups, with Haemophilus influenzae being the most common pathogen. The results suggest that empirical antibiotic therapy should be tailored to cover beta-lactamase-producing pathogens in these patients. The study's large sample size and statistical methods support its findings, though its retrospective design may introduce bias.

title: Aspergillus species isolation in respiratory samples from patients with respiratory syncytial virus: An 11-year retrospective single-center cohort study.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory syncytial virus is a significant cause of morbidity in adults, but data on fungal coinfections, beyond influenza-associated pulmonary aspergillosis and COVID-19-associated pulmonary aspergillosis, remain limited.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We conducted an 11-year retrospective study at Hospital Universitario La Paz (Madrid, Spain) including 17 adult patients with confirmed respiratory syncytial virus infection and Aspergillus isolation from respiratory samples.
analysis.methods: Episodes were classified as probable invasive aspergillosis or colonization according to clinical, radiological, and microbiological findings.
analysis.main_results: A total of 18 episodes were identified, with the species within the Aspergillus fumigatus complex being the most frequently isolated (78.9%), followed by Aspergillus terreus complex (10.5%), Aspergillus nidulans complex (5.3%), and Aspergillus niger complex (5.3). Most isolates were considered colonization (55.6%), while probable invasive aspergillosis accounted for 44.4% episodes, based on compatible clinical and radiological findings. Corticosteroid exposure was common with 82.4% receiving or starting a corticosteroid therapy during hospitalization, and antifungal therapy was administered in 44.4% of episodes, including voriconazole and liposomal amphotericin B. The median hospital stay was 16 days (IQR: 8-28). Mortality was 11.1%.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Our study provides novel insights into Aspergillus isolation associated with respiratory syncytial virus infection and emphasizes the need for further multicentric studies to define epidemiology, risk factors, and optimal management strategies.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Aspergillus isolation in adults with respiratory syncytial virus infection was observed mainly in patients with underlying pulmonary disease or comorbidities, with colonization being more frequent than invasive aspergillosis.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: However, no episodes of severe invasive aspergillosis requiring intensive care were observed in this cohort.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to characterize the isolation of Aspergillus in respiratory samples from adult patients with confirmed respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection over an 11-year period. Conducted at Hospital Universitario La Paz in Madrid, Spain, it included 17 patients with RSV infection and Aspergillus isolation. The study classified episodes as colonization or probable invasive aspergillosis based on clinical, radiological, and microbiological findings. Results showed that the Aspergillus fumigatus complex was most frequently isolated (78.9%), followed by other species. Colonization was more common than invasive aspergillosis (55.6% vs. 44.4%), with corticosteroid use and antifungal therapy observed in 82.4% and 44.4% of episodes, respectively. The median hospital stay was 16 days, and mortality was 11.1%. The authors concluded that Aspergillus isolation is more prevalent in patients with underlying pulmonary disease or comorbidities, highlighting the need for further research. However, no severe invasive aspergillosis cases requiring intensive care were observed, which may limit the generalizability of findings.

title: Decision-Making About Respiratory Syncytial Virus Immunization for Infants: Qualitative Interview Study

analysis.scope_and_question: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is the leading cause of infant hospitalization in the United States. The study aimed to examine the behavioral and social drivers shaping decisions regarding RSV vaccination during pregnancy and infant RSV monoclonal antibody immunization among pregnant individuals in the United States.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: We conducted an exploratory qualitative study from a relativist epistemological perspective, using semistructured interviews with 12 pregnant and postpartum adults recruited across the United States between October 2024 and May 2025. Interviews were guided by the World Health Organization’s behavioral and social drivers of vaccination framework and analyzed using a framework analysis approach. Screening survey data were summarized descriptively to characterize participant immunization intentions and contextualize the qualitative findings.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: RSV immunization decisions reflected interacting behavioral, emotional, social, and practical influences rather than attitudes alone. Participants consistently identified trusted clinician communication, opportunities for early discussion, and access to clear educational materials as important influences on decision-making.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Participants with unsure or negative intentions emphasized the novelty of RSV vaccines, concerns about safety and long-term effects, and greater reliance on clinician recommendations and peer experiences when making decisions. Across intention groups, participants expressed a preference for receiving protection during pregnancy rather than after birth but reported uncertainty related to vaccine availability, timing within the 32- to 36-week eligibility window, and inconsistent integration into prenatal care.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Integrating education on RSV and RSV immunization options earlier in prenatal care, strengthening clinician recommendations, and reducing logistical barriers to maternal vaccination may improve informed decision-making and timely uptake of infant RSV protection.

analysis.summary_en: This qualitative study explores the behavioral and social drivers influencing decisions about RSV immunization during pregnancy and infant RSV monoclonal antibody immunization among pregnant individuals in the United States. The research highlights that RSV immunization decisions are shaped by a complex interplay of behavioral, emotional, social, and practical factors rather than attitudes alone. Participants with positive intentions expressed greater trust in medical expertise and personal experience with RSV illness, while those with unsure or negative intentions raised concerns about vaccine safety and long-term effects. The study emphasizes the importance of early prenatal education, clinician communication, and reducing logistical barriers to improve informed decision-making and timely uptake of RSV protection strategies. The findings suggest that addressing these factors could enhance maternal vaccination rates and support better infant health outcomes.

title: Binding antibodies against respiratory syncytial virus and association with age-specific neutralizing antibodies and hospitalization patterns in Israel

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) imposes a substantial health burden, particularly in infants and older adults, but comprehensive population-level data describing age-specific antibody responses alongside hospitalization patterns are scarce.
analysis.study_design_and_population: To assess RSV seropositivity across demographic and geographic variables, to evaluate age-specific binding and neutralizing antibody responses, and to describe the age distribution of RSV-positive hospitalizations in an independent hospitalized cohort; any comparisons between the serosurvey and the hospitalized cohort are descriptive and hypothesis-generating.
analysis.methods: A cross-sectional sero-survey of 1,396 sera samples was conducted to measure RSV binding antibodies using ELISA (values were defined as high-positive, borderline or low-positive). Of them, neutralizing antibodies were assessed in 243 age-stratified sera.
analysis.main_results: Overall, the RSV high-seropositivity rate was 7.8%, with infants aged 0–12 months showing the lowest seroprevalence (0.0%) while children aged 13–59 months (15.4%) and adults aged ≥ 60 years (12.9%) showed the highest. RSV geometric mean titers (GMTs) differed significantly by age, increasing from infancy to adulthood and peaking in those aged ≥ 60 years ( p < 0.0001).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Age-specific differences in both the quantity and functional quality of antibodies were observed, with marked demographic variation.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings highlight the need for targeted vaccination and prevention strategies, particularly for high-risk groups such as infants and older adults.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Because the serosurvey and hospitalized cohort are independent, the observed concordance or discordance between antibody patterns and hospitalization distribution is descriptive and does not establish causality.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates age-specific antibody responses to Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) in Israel, highlighting the scarcity of population-level data on this topic. A cross-sectional sero-survey of 1,396 sera samples measured RSV binding antibodies using ELISA, while neutralizing antibodies were assessed in 243 age-stratified sera. The results showed that infants had the lowest seroprevalence (0.0%) and children aged 13–59 months had the highest (15.4%), with adults aged ≥ 60 years also showing high seropositivity (12.9%). RSV geometric mean titers (GMTs) increased with age, peaking in those aged ≥ 60 years. In the hospitalized cohort, infants accounted for the largest proportion of RSV-positive hospitalizations (35.3%), followed by adults aged ≥ 60 years (25.4%). The study notes that the observed patterns are descriptive and do not establish causality. These findings suggest the need for targeted vaccination and prevention strategies for high-risk groups. The study's limitations include the independence of the two datasets, which prevents linking individual-level data.

title: Subconjunctival Hemorrhage and Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infection in an Infant Evaluated for Non-accidental Trauma: A Case Report of a Possible Association

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to explore the potential association between subconjunctival hemorrhage (SCH) and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection in an infant, as SCH may be a sentinel finding for non-accidental trauma (NAT).
analysis.study_design_and_population: A case report was conducted on a six-week-old infant with a subconjunctival hemorrhage and concomitant RSV infection, evaluated for possible non-accidental trauma.
analysis.methods: An extensive multidisciplinary evaluation was performed to assess for traumatic injuries or evidence of abuse, including clinical examination and diagnostic testing for RSV infection.
analysis.main_results: The infant had a subconjunctival hemorrhage and RSV infection, but no traumatic injuries or evidence of abuse were found. The SCH resolved within one week, and the patient recovered with supportive care without complications.

title: 06 | Nirsevimab as a key strategy to prevent respiratory syncytial virus among newborns and children: real-world evidence from Italy and Sicily

analysis.scope_and_question: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is one of the leading causes of lower respiratory tract infections and hospitalization during the first year of life.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A non-systematic review of the scientific literature was conducted, focusing on real-world effectiveness (RWE) studies carried out in Italy following the introduction of Nirsevimab during the 2024/2025 season.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Real-world effectiveness data available in the scientific literature from different Italian regions have confirmed the high effectiveness of Nirsevimab observed in clinical trials, in line with findings reported in the international literature. Studies conducted in Italy have reported immunization effectiveness in real-world settings exceeding 85% in preventing severe RSV disease, over 80% in preventing RSV-related hospitalizations in neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) or pediatric wards, and over 70% in preventing emergency department visits for RSV-related illness.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The effectiveness of Nirsevimab can translate into a meaningful public health benefit only if high immunization coverage is achieved, ensuring protection for both in-season and out-of-season births, the latter currently representing a key challenge, with lower uptake rates. It is also important to document informed parental refusal among those who decline prophylaxis and to ensure re-immunization during the second RSV season for vulnerable children (i.e., the former palivizumab-eligible cohort).
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Furthermore, RespivirNet surveillance data should guide the definition of the immunization window on an annual basis, including consideration of a possible extension of immunization at birth through April 30, in view of the progressively later onset of RSV circulation at both the community and hospital levels, particularly in Southern Italian regions. In summary, nirsevimab represents not merely a new preventive strategy, but a paradigm shift: a true revolution in RSV prevention.

analysis.summary_en: This review article evaluates the real-world effectiveness of Nirsevimab in preventing respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) among newborns and children in Italy and Sicily. The study highlights that Nirsevimab, administered as a single dose, has extended protection to infants during their first RSV season, surpassing the limitations of Palivizumab. Real-world data from Italian regions confirm its high effectiveness, with reported rates exceeding 85% in preventing severe RSV disease, over 80% in preventing hospitalizations, and over 70% in reducing emergency department visits. The article emphasizes the importance of achieving high immunization coverage, particularly for out-of-season births, and suggests extending the immunization window based on surveillance data. It concludes that Nirsevimab represents a paradigm shift in RSV prevention, significantly impacting hospital and community healthcare burdens.

title: A ciliated epithelial cell line as a model for respiratory syncytial virus research

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is the leading cause of severe respiratory infection in infants and an increasingly recognized pathogen in the elderly. The study aimed to address the need for a more accurate in vitro model to study RSV infection.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study evaluated the human bronchial epithelial cell line BCi-NS1.1 differentiated at an air-liquid interface (ALI) as an alternative model for RSV research. The cell line was used to simulate in vivo conditions for studying RSV infection.
analysis.methods: The researchers differentiated the BCi-NS1.1 cell line at an air-liquid interface (ALI) and assessed its characteristics. They also generated an RSV lacking NS2, a protein promoting cell rounding and shedding, to facilitate subcellular analysis.
analysis.main_results: Three weeks after ALI differentiation, BCi-NS1.1 cultures exhibited mature tight junctions, IL-13-induced MUC5AC production, a transepithelial potential difference of around −20 mV and 19% ciliated cells. These cultures were readily infected by RSV from the apical side, with infected cell numbers increasing from day 1 to day 5 post-infection.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that ALI-differentiated BCi-NS1.1 cells provide a suitable tool for studying epithelial responses to RSV infection, as they closely mimic in vivo conditions and support RSV replication and shedding.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that BCi-NS1.1 cells differentiated at ALI can be used for studying RSV infection mechanisms, which may inform future research on diagnosis, treatment and prevention strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to in vitro observations and does not account for in vivo complexities. However, the evidence is strong as it directly reports on the characteristics and infection dynamics of RSV in a relevant cell model.

analysis.summary_en: This study introduces the human bronchial epithelial cell line BCi-NS1.1 differentiated at an air-liquid interface (ALI) as a potential in vitro model for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) research. RSV is a major cause of severe respiratory infections in infants and the elderly, and conventional cell lines lack key airway epithelial features. The ALI-differentiated BCi-NS1.1 cells showed advanced differentiation, including mature tight junctions, ciliated cells, and a transepithelial potential difference. These cells were infected by RSV from the apical side, with infected cell numbers increasing over days. The study also generated an RSV lacking NS2 to better observe subcellular processes. The authors concluded that these cells provide a suitable tool for studying RSV infection, as they closely mimic in vivo conditions. The findings are significant for future research on RSV mechanisms but are limited to in vitro observations.

title: 01 | Integrated prevention of respiratory syncytial virus in infants after the “revolution”: reflections from the first two seasons in Sicily and Calabria

analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on the prevention of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) disease in infants, particularly after the introduction of maternal immunization and monoclonal antibody prophylaxis. The central question is how these new strategies have impacted the clinical outcomes and organizational challenges in Sicily and Calabria.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The evidence base is derived from a narrative review based on a structured discussion with two healthcare professionals involved in RSV prevention. The review does not report on specific databases, search dates, or meta-analysis methods, but it includes general descriptions of the study design and population.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The first two seasons of implementation suggest a substantial reduction in the burden of severe RSV disease. The effectiveness of RSV prevention strategies depends not only on the availability of maternal immunization and monoclonal antibody prophylaxis but also on the integration of these interventions into routine care pathways.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Residual hospitalizations continue to occur, particularly among infants who did not receive timely prophylaxis, very young infants, and children with underlying vulnerabilities. The review highlights challenges in the timely identification of eligible women, coordination between maternity units and vaccination services, and the consistency of information provided by healthcare professionals.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Strengthening collaboration among maternity units, vaccination services, paediatricians, and community healthcare professionals will be essential to improve timely access, reduce residual preventable disease, and ensure equitable protection for infants in Sicily and Calabria.

analysis.summary_en: This review evaluates the impact of new RSV prevention strategies, including maternal immunization and monoclonal antibody prophylaxis, in Sicily and Calabria during the first two seasons of implementation. It highlights a significant reduction in severe RSV disease burden but also notes ongoing challenges in organizational delivery and residual cases among vulnerable infants. The review emphasizes the need for improved coordination and communication to ensure equitable protection and timely access to these interventions.

title: Health and Economic Burden of Severe Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infections Among Older Adults in Japan: A Retrospective Administrative Database Study

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to assess the health and economic burden of severe respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections in older adults in Japan, as the incidence and disease burden of RSV in this population is likely underestimated due to the lack of routine testing and surveillance.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective cohort study was conducted using data from the Medical Data Vision (MDV) hospital-based claims database and the insurance-based JMDC database, covering the period from 1 September 2008 to 31 August 2021. The study included 178 cases of RSV infection, with 144 from the MDV database and 34 from the JMDC database, focusing on adults aged ≥ 60 years.
analysis.methods: Data were collected from two anonymized health claims databases, and comparisons were analyzed using a paired sample t-test with statistical significance set at p < 0.05. Healthcare resource utilization (HCRU) and medical costs were compared between pre- and post-event periods.
analysis.main_results: In the MDV cohort, the average number of outpatient visits increased from 1.21 to 2.07, and hospitalizations increased from 0.07 to 0.37 within 30 days post-event, resulting in significant additional medical costs of ¥196,231 (p < 0.001). The impact decreased over time, with no statistical significance detected in the 365-day post-event period. The number of RSV cases increased over the study period, reaching 38 and 36 cases in 2018–2019 and 2019–2020, respectively.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings highlight the significant health and economic burden of RSV infections in older adults, emphasizing the need for targeted interventions such as vaccination, especially given Japan’s aging population.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The study provides critical insights into the healthcare resource utilization and costs associated with RSV infections in older adults, supporting the development of strategies for surveillance, prevention, and management in this vulnerable group.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on administrative databases, which may lack detailed clinical information. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the observational nature of the study and potential for unmeasured confounding factors.

analysis.summary_en: This retrospective cohort study examined the health and economic burden of severe respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections in older adults in Japan using data from two health claims databases. The study found that RSV infections led to a significant increase in healthcare resource utilization and medical costs within 30 days of diagnosis, with the impact diminishing over time. These findings underscore the importance of addressing RSV in older populations, particularly given the high proportion of Japan’s aging population. The study's reliance on administrative data limits its depth, and the evidence is considered moderate due to the observational design and potential for confounding factors.

title: Albumin-to-alkaline phosphatase ratio as an immuno-metabolic marker of bacterial co-infection phenotype in pediatric RSV infection: insights from protein–protein interaction networks

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection in children is frequently complicated by bacterial co-infection, which significantly aggravates clinical outcomes. This study aimed to investigate the association between AAPR and Gram-positive (G + ) versus Gram-negative (G-) bacterial co-infection phenotypes among RSV-infected children, evaluate its discriminative performance, and explore potentially relevant biological pathways.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We retrospectively analyzed 153 pediatric patients with laboratory-confirmed RSV and bacterial co-infection. The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Second Affiliated Hospital and Yuying Children’s Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University.
analysis.methods: Multivariable logistic regression and restricted cubic spline (RCS) analyses were employed to determine the independent association and dose-response relationship between AAPR and infection phenotypes. Diagnostic performance was quantified using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). An exploratory systems biology analysis was performed to identify candidate genes and signaling pathways potentially relevant to the observed association.
analysis.main_results: Multivariable logistic regression demonstrated that elevated AAPR was independently and inversely associated with the likelihood of G+ infection (OR = 0.37; 95% CI: 0.15–0.89 for the highest vs. RCS analysis showed no evidence of a nonlinear association (P for non-linearity = 0.456). AAPR alone showed modest discriminative performance (AUC = 0.599). Addition of AAPR to CRP, WBC, and NEU increased the AUC from 0.455 to 0.613; however, the difference did not reach the conventional threshold for statistical significance (P = 0.051).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The Albumin-to-Alkaline Phosphatase Ratio (AAPR) has recently emerged as a novel immuno-metabolic marker. Exploratory systems biology analysis identified IL-17-, TNF-, and other inflammation-related pathways as candidates for further investigation.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings may inform the development of immuno-metabolic markers for early detection of bacterial co-infection in RSV-infected children. These insights could contribute to improved diagnostic strategies and targeted therapeutic approaches.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The association was attenuated after normalization using age-specific pediatric ALP reference limits, and the difference in AUC did not reach the conventional threshold for statistical significance. The study is retrospective and based on de-identified clinical data, which may introduce bias and limit generalizability.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the association between the Albumin-to-Alkaline Phosphatase Ratio (AAPR) and bacterial co-infection phenotypes in children with Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) infection. The research highlights the potential of AAPR as an immuno-metabolic marker for distinguishing Gram-positive from Gram-negative bacterial co-infections. Results show an inverse association between elevated AAPR and G+ infection, though this was attenuated after normalization. AAPR demonstrated modest discriminative performance, and its addition to standard markers like CRP, WBC, and NEU slightly improved diagnostic accuracy without reaching statistical significance. The study also identified inflammation-related pathways as candidates for further investigation. However, limitations include the retrospective design and potential bias from de-identified data, which may affect generalizability. The evidence is moderate in strength, with findings grounded in statistical analysis and systems biology approaches.

title: RSV: A Training-Free Verification Framework for Proactive and Efficient Online Video Understanding

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the limitations of current online Video Large Language Models (Video-LLMs) in handling the dense spatiotemporal redundancy of continuous video streams, which hinders their proactive responsiveness and inference efficiency.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study introduced a training-free framework called Reference State Verification (RSV) to transform pre-trained offline Video-LLMs into proactive online assistants, focusing on the challenges of managing continuous visual data streams.
analysis.methods: The framework utilizes semantic state comparison to enable proactive decision-making, and it introduces Attention Distribution Divergence (ADD) as a verification signal based on cross-modal attention deviation. Additionally, Verification-guided Spatio-Temporal Compression (VSTC) re-purposes these signals for redundancy elimination through semantic-guided frame dropping and spatial token pruning.
analysis.main_results: Extensive experiments showed that the plug-and-play approach significantly improves the inference efficiency and proactive responsiveness of various Video-LLMs without requiring architectural changes or parameter fine-tuning.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret their findings as demonstrating a novel, training-free method that enhances the performance of Video-LLMs by addressing the challenges of continuous video stream processing through semantic state comparison and verification signals.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the development of more efficient and autonomous video understanding systems, which may have applications in real-time monitoring and analysis of video content for public health and scientific research.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to abstract-level evidence and does not provide detailed experimental results or statistical analyses. The evidence strength is moderate as it is based on general claims about the framework's performance.

analysis.summary_en: This study introduces a training-free framework called Reference State Verification (RSV) to enhance the proactive responsiveness and inference efficiency of Video Large Language Models (Video-LLMs) in handling continuous video streams. The framework utilizes semantic state comparison and introduces Attention Distribution Divergence (ADD) as a verification signal based on cross-modal attention deviation. Additionally, Verification-guided Spatio-Temporal Compression (VSTC) re-purposes these signals for redundancy elimination through semantic-guided frame dropping and spatial token pruning. The authors interpret their findings as demonstrating a novel approach that improves Video-LLMs without requiring architectural modifications or parameter fine-tuning. The study's results can inform the development of more efficient video understanding systems, which may have applications in public health and scientific research. However, the evidence is limited to abstract-level descriptions, and the study does not provide detailed experimental results or statistical analyses, resulting in moderate confidence in the findings.

title: Clinically relevant RSV anti-F antibodies exhibit comparable inhibition of syncytium formation despite marked differences in neutralization potency

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate the ability of clinically relevant anti-RSV F monoclonal antibodies to inhibit syncytium formation, addressing the gap in understanding their functional properties beyond conventional virus neutralization assays.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used a quantitative flow cytometry-based assay to measure RSV-induced syncytium formation in HEp-2 and A549 cells, comparing clinically relevant anti-F mAbs.
analysis.methods: A novel quantitative flow cytometry-based assay was developed to measure syncytium formation, and clinically relevant anti-F mAbs were evaluated for their potency in syncytium inhibition and conventional virus neutralization assays.
analysis.main_results: Palivizumab, nirsevimab, and clesrovimab inhibited syncytium formation in a dose-dependent manner, with only modest differences in potency, while nirsevimab and clesrovimab exhibited substantially greater virus neutralization potency than palivizumab.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings indicate that inhibition of RSV-induced cell-to-cell fusion represents a distinct functional property of anti-F antibodies that is not fully captured by conventional neutralization assays, highlighting the value of complementary functional readouts.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The study provides insights into the functional properties of anti-F antibodies and underscores the need for complementary assays to fully evaluate their efficacy in preventing RSV infection and disease.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by the use of only two cell lines and the absence of direct clinical correlation, suggesting that the findings may not fully generalize to all RSV infections.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the ability of clinically relevant anti-RSV F monoclonal antibodies to inhibit syncytium formation using a novel quantitative flow cytometry-based assay, demonstrating that these antibodies have distinct functional properties beyond conventional virus neutralization assays.

title: Public Health Impact of Universal Nirsevimab Prophylaxis: A Multicenter Study on the Reduction of RSV Hospitalizations in Infants in Tuscany, Italy.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Nirsevimab is a long-acting monoclonal antibody approved for the prevention of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) lower respiratory tract disease in infants. Although growing real-world evidence supports its effectiveness, large multicenter studies assessing the population-level impact of universal immunization remain limited.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We conducted a multicenter retrospective study involving nearly the entire pediatric hospital network in Tuscany, Italy. The public health impact of the universal nirsevimab program was assessed through a pre-post comparison of the 2023-24 and 2024-25 RSV seasons. This large multicenter study demonstrates a major population-level impact and high real-world effectiveness.
analysis.methods: Nirsevimab effectiveness against RSV-associated hospitalization was estimated using the screening method.
analysis.main_results: RSV-related hospitalizations declined from 533 cases in 2023-24 to 104 in 2024-25, corresponding to an 80.5% reduction (IRR 0.20, 95% CI 0.16-0.24; p<0.001). Significant reductions were observed across all markers of disease severity, respiratory support requirements and healthcare utilization, including PICU admissions (-87.0%), low-flow oxygen therapy (-78.7%), high-flow oxygen therapy (-81.0%), non-invasive ventilation (-85.0%), bronchodilator use (-82.3%), corticosteroid use (-89.3%), and antibiotic therapy (-84.5%).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Universal nirsevimab immunization was associated with substantial reductions in RSV-related hospitalizations, disease severity, and healthcare resource utilization across Tuscany. Breakthrough hospitalizations occurred throughout the RSV season and did not show a progressive increase across longer post-administration intervals, although the available data do not allow a formal assessment of waning protection.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings underscore the important contribution of infants born outside the traditional RSV season to the overall RSV burden, supporting prevention strategies that protect the entire birth cohort. The results suggest that universal nirsevimab immunization could significantly reduce the public health burden of RSV in infants.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The findings do not constitute a formal evaluation of durability of protection, and the available data do not allow a formal assessment of waning protection. The evidence is strong, with a high confidence level due to the large multicenter study design and clear pre-post comparisons.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluates the public health impact of universal nirsevimab prophylaxis in infants in Tuscany, Italy, during the 2023-24 and 2024-25 RSV seasons. A multicenter retrospective study design was used to compare RSV-related hospitalizations and healthcare resource utilization before and after the implementation of the nirsevimab program. The results show a substantial reduction in RSV-related hospitalizations, with an 80.5% decline and an estimated effectiveness of 89.7% against RSV-associated hospitalization. Disease severity markers and respiratory support requirements also decreased significantly. The study highlights the importance of protecting infants born outside the traditional RSV season and suggests that universal immunization could reduce the overall burden of RSV. However, the study does not formally assess the durability of protection, and the evidence is strong due to the large sample size and clear pre-post comparisons.

title: Transplacental transfer efficiency and longitudinal dynamics of antibodies against RSV in early childhood: a paired mother-neonate cohort study in southern China.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Maternal antibodies provide early-life protection against severe respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection but wane rapidly. With the availability of maternal vaccine and half-life extended monoclonal antibodies for infants, understanding transplacental antibody transfer and subsequent antibody dynamics is important for optimising immunisation strategies.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We conducted a longitudinal cohort study of 695 mother-neonate pairs in southern China between 2013 and 2021. Serum samples were collected from mothers at delivery and from children at birth, 2, 4, 6, 12, 24, 36 months, and 5-8 years of age.
analysis.methods: All samples were tested for RSV pre-F IgG antibodies using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. A subset of samples was additionally tested for neutralizing antibodies (nAbs) using a foci reduction neutralization test.
analysis.main_results: Maternal and cord blood RSV pre-F IgG antibody levels were positively correlated (= 0.87; P<0.001) with a mean transplacental transfer ratio of 1.44 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.40-1.47). Maternally derived antibodies declined rapidly after birth, with an estimated half-life of 34.3 days (95% CI, 33.9-34.8); antibody levels reached a nadir at approximately 10 months of age and gradually increased thereafter.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Our findings highlight the importance of addressing lower maternally derived antibody levels in preterm infants, particularly in the context of maternal immunisation. Longitudinal antibody dynamics reveal a distinct period of low antibody levels during infancy that may inform the timing of targeted RSV immunisation strategies.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings may inform the timing of targeted RSV immunisation strategies, particularly for preterm infants who have lower maternally derived antibody levels. Understanding antibody dynamics can help optimise immunisation strategies for infants.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on serum samples and the potential for confounding factors, but the evidence is strong with a high confidence level due to the large sample size and longitudinal design.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the transplacental transfer efficiency and longitudinal dynamics of antibodies against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in early childhood, focusing on a paired mother-neonate cohort in southern China. The research highlights the rapid waning of maternal antibodies and the importance of addressing lower antibody levels in preterm infants. It also reveals a distinct period of low antibody levels during infancy, which may inform the timing of targeted RSV immunisation strategies. The study's findings are supported by a robust methodology involving longitudinal sampling and testing for both IgG and neutralizing antibodies. However, the study's reliance on serum samples and potential confounding factors may limit the generalisability of its results. The evidence is strong and has high confidence due to the large sample size and comprehensive analysis of antibody dynamics.

title: Epidemiology of acute respiratory infections in adult patients in Hospices Civils de Lyon, France, between October 2016 and April 2025

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to describe viral circulation among adult patients with acute respiratory infections (ARI) in France, addressing the need to understand the impact of multiple viruses on morbidity, mortality, and hospital resources.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective cohort study was conducted using electronic health records from the Hospices Civils de Lyon, France, involving adult patients (≥18 years) hospitalised or presenting to the emergency department from October 2016 to April 2025 with either an ICD-10 diagnostic code for ARI or a laboratory-confirmed viral detection.
analysis.methods: Methods included the assembly of a retrospective cohort using electronic health records, extraction of administrative variables and laboratory results during the hospital stay, and analysis of data from October 2016 to April 2025.
analysis.main_results: The study included 103,011 hospital visits involving 82,077 patients, with a substantial increase in eligible stays since the COVID-19 pandemic, along with year-round laboratory testing. Winter peaks of ARI incidence, influenza, and RSV detections re-emerged after 2022.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study found that influenza, rhinovirus, and SARS-CoV-2 positivity rates peaked in younger adults (<65 years), whereas RSV and hMPV positivity rates were highest in patients aged ≥80 years. Patients aged ≥65 years had longer hospitalisations, higher mortality rates, and less frequent ICU admission and respiratory support compared to younger adults.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform surveillance of viral circulation, early identification of patients at risk of deterioration, and evaluation of the impact of preventive interventions in the community.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design, potential for bias in data collection, and the lack of specific RSV data, which may affect the generalisability of the findings.

analysis.summary_en: This study described the viral circulation among adult patients with acute respiratory infections in France, highlighting the impact of various viruses on patient outcomes and hospital resources. The findings can inform surveillance and preventive interventions.

title: Viral Aetiology of Lower Respiratory Tract Infections in Infants Attending Primary Care in Eastern Spain, 2023-2025.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to understand the seasonal patterns of respiratory viruses in infants following the implementation of an RSV-immunisation programme in Spain, focusing on the impact of this intervention on viral aetiology.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study analysed multiplex RT-PCR results from 307 infants under 1 year of age with lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) attending 57 primary care centres in Valencia and Murcia over two seasons.
analysis.methods: The researchers used multiplex RT-PCR to detect respiratory viruses in infants with LRTIs, focusing on seasonal patterns post-RSV immunisation programme rollout.
analysis.main_results: Among the 307 infants, rhinovirus/enterovirus and RSV were the most common detections in both periods, with hMPV, bocavirus, and influenza following.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that community-based surveillance systems are crucial for generating real-world evidence to guide future immunisation strategies.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results provide insights into the changing dynamics of respiratory virus infections in infants, which can inform public health planning and immunisation strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to two seasons and focuses on primary care settings, which may affect generalisability. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the observational nature of the study.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the seasonal patterns of respiratory viruses in infants under one year of age attending primary care centres in Valencia and Murcia, Spain, following the rollout of an RSV-immunisation programme. Multiplex RT-PCR was used to detect viral aetiology in 307 infants with lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) over two seasons. The most common detections were rhinovirus/enterovirus and RSV, with hMPV, bocavirus, and influenza also identified. The findings highlight the importance of community-based surveillance systems in providing real-world evidence to inform future immunisation strategies. The study's limitations include its focus on two seasons and primary care settings, which may limit generalisability. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the observational design and the absence of control groups.

title: Epidemiological Characteristics and Antimicrobial Resistance Profiles of Haemophilus influenzae Respiratory Infections in Hospitalized Children: A 7-Year Retrospective Study in Kunming

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to analyze the epidemiological characteristics and antimicrobial resistance profiles of Haemophilus influenzae respiratory infections in hospitalized children to provide evidence for local prevention and rational antibiotic selection.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This retrospective study included hospitalized children diagnosed with Haemophilus influenzae respiratory tract infection in Kunming from 2019 to 2025.
analysis.methods: The researchers stratified and summarized epidemiological characteristics, co-infecting pathogens and antimicrobial susceptibility results based on age group, month, season and gender.
analysis.main_results: A total of 11,217 cases were confirmed by sputum culture or PCR. Annual case numbers fluctuated and increased overall, reaching the lowest level in 2020 and the highest in 2024–2025, with obvious concentration in winter and spring. The proportion of preschool and school-aged children gradually increased, whereas that of infants declined significantly (P < 0.001). Although boys were still predominant, the proportion of girls rose year by year.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors concluded that paediatric Haemophilus influenzae respiratory infections present a winter-spring bimodal epidemic and an age shift toward older children.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that continuous local surveillance and susceptibility data should guide clinical antibiotic use.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is retrospective and may be subject to biases, but the evidence is strong due to the large sample size and comprehensive data collection.

analysis.summary_en: This 7-year retrospective study in Kunming analyzed Haemophilus influenzae respiratory infections in hospitalized children, focusing on epidemiological patterns and antimicrobial resistance. It found that case numbers fluctuated, with peaks in winter and spring, and a shift toward older children. The study highlights the importance of local surveillance for guiding antibiotic use. While the study is retrospective and may have biases, the large sample size and detailed data collection support its findings.

title: An Interferon-Braked Monocyte State and Compartment-Specific Myeloid Programming Across Severe Respiratory Infections

analysis.research_question_and_background: Severe COVID-19 is accompanied by marked remodeling of airway myeloid compartments, yet how infiltrating monocytes are routed toward inflammatory versus pro-fibrotic fates, and why resident alveolar macrophages fail to recover, remains incompletely understood.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We re-analyzed BALF single-cell data (GSE145926; 3 healthy, 3 mild/moderate, 6 severe; 27,807 cells), re-clustering myeloid cells (n = 19,485) into 37 fine states (13 families) with functional module scoring, diffusion pseudotime, PAGA, a curated ligand–receptor screen, and per-donor decomposition; validation used the independent fatal-COVID-19 BALF cohort GSE157344 and the healthy-BALF cohort GSE151928 as a specificity control, a human endotoxin bone-marrow comparator (GSE212092), two sepsis blood cohorts (GSE175453; GSE167363, paired 0 h/6 h), three cross-pathogen blood cohorts (influenza A GSE243629, infant RSV GSE283746, bacterial ARDS GSE157789), and cross-disease comparison with IPF lung (GSE128033).
analysis.methods: Healthy BALF comprised resident alveolar macrophages, depleted in severe disease and replaced by interferon-activated, CXCL8-high, and SPP1+ populations. A CD14+SPP1−FCN1+ population co-expressing interferon-stimulated genes and IL1RN—an interferon-braked state distinct from LPS-type trained immunity—was enriched in severe disease, driven predominantly by one patient. PAGA delineated an FCN1+→intermediate→SPP1+ continuum; severe-enriched circuits included MIF–CD74 and an autocrine CXCL8–CXCR2 loop.
analysis.main_results: The interferon-braked signature and SPP1+ compartments were reproduced in an independent fatal-COVID-19 BALF cohort and were at baseline in a healthy-BALF reference cohort (0.343 ± 0.091); LPS-challenged marrow showed the reciprocal pattern (TLR4-high, interferon-silent); and IPF lung shared SPP1/TREM2 induction with resident-AM collapse (SPP1 p = 0.0005). In sepsis blood, monocytes retained the interferon-braked signature with the LPS/TLR4 module near baseline; the signature was likewise elevated in bacterial ARDS, influenza A, and infant RSV monocytes, extending the compartment model beyond COVID-19.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The data support a two-signal model: interferon restrains recruited monocytes at entry, while TLR4/HIF-1α- and SPP1-associated programs act downstream. The brake state is a measurable, stage-specific marker; MIF–CD74, CXCL8–CXCR2, and SPP1–CD44 are candidate nodes for stage-specific intervention. These mechanistic interpretations are grounded in the data and are proposed as testable hypotheses.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings could inform surveillance, diagnosis, and treatment of severe respiratory infections, including COVID-19, by identifying a measurable, stage-specific marker for interferon-braked monocytes. This could aid in understanding and managing the progression of severe respiratory diseases.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by the use of single-cell data from BALF, which may not fully capture systemic responses. The findings are specific to the context of severe respiratory infections and may not generalize to other diseases or settings. The evidence strength is moderate due to the observational nature of the study and the need for further validation in larger, more diverse cohorts.

analysis.summary_en: This study re-analyzed single-cell data from BALF to understand the fate of monocytes in severe respiratory infections, identifying an interferon-braked state that could be a marker for severe disease. The findings suggest a two-signal model and propose testable hypotheses for intervention.

title: Dual-aptamer magnetic capture and electrochemical detection of influenza B and respiratory syncytial viruses in artificial saliva.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Saliva is a promising non-invasive specimen for respiratory virus diagnostics but its biochemical complexity challenges direct interfacing with affinity-based biosensors.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We report a dual-aptamer magnetic-capture electrochemical assay for detection of influenza B virus (IBV) and human respiratory syncytial virus (hRSV) in artificial saliva.
analysis.methods: For each target virus, two sequence-distinct DNA aptamers are used: an amino-modified capture aptamer (IBV1 or RSV1) covalently coupled to ∼5 μm polydopamine-coated magnetic microparticles by direct Schiff-base reaction with the polydopamine quinone/catechol surface, and a thiol-modified detection aptamer (IBV2 or RSV2) self-assembled on screen-printed gold electrodes via thiol-gold chemistry.
analysis.main_results: After a single multiplexed batch capture step with both aptamer-magnetic-particle types, the pellet is split and analysed in parallel on the two aptamer-modified electrodes by square-wave voltammetry (SWV).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Langmuir analysis of the SWV calibration curves yielded apparent dissociation constants of Kd = 177 ± 62 PFU mL-1 (IBV) and 226 ± 85 PFU mL-1 (hRSV), with detection limits of 15 and 11 PFU mL-1, respectively.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The sequence-orthogonal dual-aptamer geometry-capture and detection recognitions targeting non-identical epitopes-is proposed as the structural mitigation.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: This proof-of-concept establishes a programmable, saliva-compatible architecture reconfigurable for emerging respiratory pathogens by aptamer substitution alone.

analysis.summary_en: This study presents a dual-aptamer magnetic capture and electrochemical detection method for identifying influenza B virus (IBV) and human respiratory syncytial virus (hRSV) in artificial saliva. The approach uses sequence-distinct DNA aptamers for capture and detection, with the capture aptamer attached to magnetic microparticles and the detection aptamer on gold electrodes. The method enables parallel analysis of both viruses after a single capture step. The results show apparent dissociation constants of Kd = 177 ± 62 PFU mL-1 for IBV and 226 ± 85 PFU mL-1 for hRSV, with detection limits of 15 and 11 PFU mL-1, respectively. The authors propose this method as a structural mitigation strategy for non-invasive virus detection, highlighting its potential for reconfiguration to detect emerging respiratory pathogens. The study is a proof-of-concept and does not address limitations or evidence strength directly.
